1

The upgrade: from one dot to the whole curve

In Unit 1 you solved problems like “$p_x = 3$, endowment $\omega = (10, 10)$, find the bundle” — and the answer was one point. Unit 2 asks a bigger question: what does the consumer choose at every possible price? Answering it takes no new math — just a new interpretation. Run the exact same tangency-plus-budget (or kink, or corner) recipe, but leave $p_x$, $p_y$ and the endowment $\omega = (\omega_x, \omega_y)$ as letters. The solution is the same — but the answer now changes as each variable changes.

$$x^*(p_x,\, p_y,\, \omega) \;=\; \text{the } \textbf{demand function} \text{ for } x, \qquad \text{budget: } p_x x + p_y y = \underbrace{p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y}_{W,\ \text{wealth}}$$

The demand curve is what you get when you graph $x^*$ against its own price $p_x$, holding $p_y$ and $\omega$ frozen (“ceteris paribus”). By convention economists put price on the vertical axis — blame Alfred Marshall.

Endowment vocabulary — used on every tab
  • Wealth $W = p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y$: the market value of what she owns. Unlike money income $m$, it moves when prices move.
  • Gross demand $x^*$: how much she ends up consuming. Net demand $x^* - \omega_x$: how much she buys ($>0$, a net buyer) or sells ($<0$, a net seller) in the market.
  • Autarky price: the $p_x$ at which $x^* = \omega_x$ — she keeps exactly what she started with and trades nothing. The endowment point is always affordable, so the demand curve always passes through $x = \omega_x$ at that price.

Movement along vs. shift — the definition. The demand graph plots one relationship: how $x^*$ responds to its own price $p_x$. Because $p_x$ is already an axis of the graph, changing $p_x$ changes nothing about the curve — it only changes where on the curve you are. That is a movement along. Everything else ($p_y$, $\omega_x$, $\omega_y$) is frozen background baked into the curve's position — when one of those changes, the curve is redrawn. That is a shift. Endowment twist: raising $p_x$ also raises $W$ (she owns some $x$), but that is still a movement along — the wealth change is caused by $p_x$, and $p_x$ is on the axis.

2

Intro econ's demand line — same two moves

Before deriving anything from utility, here is the demand curve the way an intro course hands it to you — already a straight line, with wealth $W$ standing in for income:

$$x^*(p_x,\, p_y,\, W) \;=\; 20 + \frac{W}{12} + 2p_y - 6p_x$$

Read the movement-vs-shift rule straight off the formula. The $-6p_x$ term is the slope relationship the graph draws: pick a $p_x$, get an $x^*$ — changing $p_x$ just picks a different point on the same line, and the negative sign in front is the Law of Demand (as $p_x$ rises, $x^*$ falls). The other two terms, $\tfrac{W}{12}$ and $2p_y$, are baked into the intercept: change $W$ (a bigger endowment) or $p_y$ and the whole line is redrawn — a shift. At the baseline $W = 120$, $p_y = 2$ the line is $x^* = 34 - 6p_x$.

3

Plan of attack. The four technique tabs re-derive demand for each utility type you already know, always with weights $a, b \neq 1$ so you can watch where they land, and always from an endowment. Every technique tab ends with its own drag-it visualizer (a dotted copper line marks $\omega_x$, so you can see net buying vs. net selling), and Curves & Shifts puts all four types side by side. Mixed practice at the end — shuffled, as always.

TypeUnit 1 recipeWhat demand looks like with an endowment

1

Cobb–Douglas demand: the share rule grows up

The shape

Concept
$$U = x^{a}y^{b} \;\Longrightarrow\; x^* = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{W}{p_x} = \frac{a}{a+b}\left(\omega_x + \frac{p_y\,\omega_y}{p_x}\right), \qquad y^* = \frac{b}{a+b}\cdot\frac{W}{p_y}$$

This is the share rule from Unit 1 wearing its real name: a demand function. She spends the fixed share $\tfrac{a}{a+b}$ of her wealth on $x$. Two features to memorize because exams love them: (1) with an endowment, $p_y$ does appear in the demand for $x$ — not through tastes, but because $p_y$ sets the value of her $\omega_y$ (a wealth effect); and (2) as $p_x \to \infty$, $x^*$ does not go to zero — it flattens out at $\tfrac{a}{a+b}\omega_x$. She always keeps her share of what she started with.

Worked example

Worked Example
Given
  • $U = x^{2}y^{3}$, endowment $\omega = (10, 10)$ — leave $p_x$, $p_y$ as letters
  • Find the demand functions $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ and $y^*(p_x, p_y)$, trace the demand curve for $p_y = 2$ at $p_x = 2, 4, 8$, and find the autarky price.
1

Tangency with letters. MRS $= -\dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y} = -\dfrac{2y}{3x}$; set the slope of the IC equal to the slope of the budget, $-\dfrac{p_x}{p_y}$:

$$\frac{2y}{3x} = \frac{p_x}{p_y} \;\Longrightarrow\; y = \frac{3p_x}{2p_y}\,x$$

2

Into the budget $p_x x + p_y y = p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y = 10p_x + 10p_y$:

$$p_x x + p_y\!\left(\frac{3p_x}{2p_y}x\right) = \frac{5}{2}\,p_x x = 10p_x + 10p_y$$

The $p_y$ on the left cancels (as it did with income) — but the $10p_y$ on the right is wealth, and it survives.

3

Solve for $x$ — this is the demand function:

$$x^*(p_x, p_y) = \frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{10p_x + 10p_y}{p_x} = 4 + \frac{4p_y}{p_x}, \qquad y^*(p_x, p_y) = \frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{10p_x + 10p_y}{p_y} = 6 + \frac{6p_x}{p_y}$$

Exactly the share rule: fractions $\tfrac{2}{5}$ and $\tfrac{3}{5}$ of wealth $W = 10p_x + 10p_y$, divided by own price.

4

Trace the curve at $p_y = 2$: $\;x^* = 4 + \dfrac{8}{p_x}$.

$$p_x = 2 \Rightarrow x^* = 8, \qquad p_x = 4 \Rightarrow x^* = 6, \qquad p_x = 8 \Rightarrow x^* = 5$$

Three dots on the same demand curve — and all three are below $\omega_x = 10$: at these prices she is a net seller of $x$, selling $2$, $4$, then $5$ units.

5

Autarky price. Set $x^* = \omega_x$: $\;4 + \dfrac{4p_y}{p_x} = 10 \Rightarrow p_x = \dfrac{2}{3}p_y$. At $p_y = 2$ that is $p_x = \tfrac{4}{3}$. Below it she is a net buyer of $x$; above it, a net seller. The demand curve passes through $(x, p_x) = (10, \tfrac{4}{3})$ no matter what.

Where the weights go: $a$ and $b$ survive only as the wealth share $\tfrac{a}{a+b}$. They never multiply the price. And notice the floor: $x^* = 4 + 4p_y/p_x \geq 4 = \tfrac{2}{5}\omega_x$. No price is high enough to make her sell more than $6$ of her $10$ units.

Your turn

Practice
Given — Problem 1
  • $U = x^{3/5}y^{2/5}$, $\;\omega = (5, 10)$. Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$, then evaluate at $p_y = 1$ for $p_x = 1, 2, 3$. At which of these prices is she a net buyer of $x$?

Share of good $x$ is $\dfrac{3/5}{3/5+2/5} = \dfrac{3}{5}$, wealth is $W = 5p_x + 10p_y$, so $x^* = \dfrac{3}{5}\cdot\dfrac{5p_x + 10p_y}{p_x} = 3 + \dfrac{6p_y}{p_x}$. At $p_y=1$: $x^* = 3 + \dfrac{6}{p_x}$.

$$p_x = 1 \Rightarrow 9, \qquad p_x = 2 \Rightarrow 6, \qquad p_x = 3 \Rightarrow 5$$

$\omega_x = 5$, so she is a net buyer at $p_x = 1$ and $2$ (buys $4$, then $1$), and exactly at autarky when $p_x = 3$.

Given — Problem 2
  • $U = x^{2}y^{2}$, $\;\omega = (8, 4)$. Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ and evaluate at $p_y = 2$ for $p_x = 1, 2, 4$. Does $p_y$ appear in your formula? Why, when it didn't with money income?

Equal weights $\Rightarrow$ share $\tfrac{1}{2}$: $\;x^* = \dfrac{8p_x + 4p_y}{2p_x} = 4 + \dfrac{2p_y}{p_x}$. At $p_y=2$: $x^* = 4 + \dfrac{4}{p_x} \Rightarrow 8,\ 6,\ 5$. Yes, $p_y$ is there: it prices her $4$ units of $y$, so it changes her wealth. With money income $m$ there was nothing for $p_y$ to re-price.

$$\boxed{x^* = 4 + \tfrac{2p_y}{p_x}}$$

2

From formula to picture

You just derived $x^* = \tfrac{2}{5}\!\left(\omega_x + \dfrac{p_y\omega_y}{p_x}\right) = 4 + \dfrac{4p_y}{p_x}$ for $U = x^2y^3$, $\omega = (10,10)$. Read the formula like a forecast of the graph: $p_x$ sits in a denominator, so as $p_x$ rises, $x^*$ falls — the Law of Demand, straight from the algebra — but only down to the floor of $4$. The endowment sits in the numerator, so a bigger endowment drags the whole curve outward — a shift. And $p_y$ multiplies $\omega_y$, so a pricier $y$ makes her richer and shifts the curve out too.

3

1

Quasilinear demand: the endowment drops out

The shape

Concept
$$u = v(x) + \beta y, \quad \text{e.g. } u = A\sqrt{x} + \beta y \;\Longrightarrow\; x^*(p_x, p_y) = \left(\frac{A\,p_y}{2\beta\,p_x}\right)^{\!2} \qquad (\text{no } \omega \text{ anywhere})$$

Unit 1's “settled appetite” becomes a demand function with a missing ingredient: the endowment is not an argument. Tangency alone pins down $x^*$, so a consumer born with a lot and one born with a little consume the same $x$ — every extra unit of wealth flows to $y$. Her wealth only shows up in $y^* = \dfrac{W - p_x x^*}{p_y}$. (Fine print: this needs $W$ large enough to afford $x^*$ in the first place; we'll stay in that region.)

Worked example

Worked Example
Given
  • $u = 12\sqrt{x} + 2y$, $\;\omega = (4, 20)$ — keep $p_x$, $p_y$ as letters
  • Find $x^*(p_x, p_y)$, then trace the demand curve for $p_y = 2$ at $p_x = 2, 3, 6$. Then get $y^*$ at $p_x = 2$, and find the autarky price.
1

Marginal utilities. $MU_x = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{x}}$, $\;MU_y = 2$, so MRS $= -\dfrac{MU_x}{MU_y} = -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{x}}$ — the weight on $y$ has been divided out.

2

Tangency with letters (slope of IC = slope of budget):

$$\frac{3}{\sqrt{x}} = \frac{p_x}{p_y} \;\Longrightarrow\; \sqrt{x} = \frac{3p_y}{p_x} \;\Longrightarrow\; x^*(p_x, p_y) = \frac{9p_y^2}{p_x^2}$$

The endowment never entered — the budget wasn't needed to find $x^*$.

3

Trace the curve at $p_y = 2$: $\;x^* = \dfrac{36}{p_x^2}$.

$$p_x = 2 \Rightarrow 9, \qquad p_x = 3 \Rightarrow 4, \qquad p_x = 6 \Rightarrow 1$$

4

$y^*$ mops up the wealth. At $p_x = 2$, $p_y = 2$: $W = 2(4) + 2(20) = 48$. Spending on $x$ is $2 \times 9 = 18$, so $y^* = \dfrac{48 - 18}{2} = 15$. She sold $5$ units of $y$ to buy $5$ extra units of $x$: net buyer of $x$.

5

Autarky price. $x^* = \omega_x \Rightarrow \dfrac{36}{p_x^2} = 4 \Rightarrow p_x = 3$. Check the trace: at $p_x = 3$ she consumes exactly her $4$ units; at $p_x = 6$ she sells $3$ of them.

Signature to quote on exams: quasilinear demand for $x$ depends only on the price ratio — give her $100$ more units of $y$ and $x^*$ doesn't budge; all of it lands on $y$. This is why quasilinear preferences make consumer surplus clean later in the course.

Your turn

Practice
Given — Problem 1
  • $u = 16\sqrt{x} + 4y$, $\;\omega = (4, 12)$. Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$, then evaluate at $p_y = 4$ for $p_x = 2, 4, 8$. Find $y^*$ at $p_x = 2$.

$MU_x = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{x}}$, $MU_y = 4 \Rightarrow$ MRS $= -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}}$; tangency $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \Rightarrow x^* = \left(\dfrac{2p_y}{p_x}\right)^2$. At $p_y = 4$: $x^* = \dfrac{64}{p_x^2} \Rightarrow 16,\ 4,\ 1$. At $p_x = 2$: $W = 8 + 48 = 56$, spending on $x$ is $32$, so $y^* = \dfrac{56-32}{4} = 6$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \left(\tfrac{2p_y}{p_x}\right)^{2}}$$

Given — Problem 2
  • $u = 10\ln x + 2y$, $\;\omega = (2, 10)$. Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ and evaluate at $p_y = 2$ for $p_x = 2, 5, 10$. Find $y^*$ at $p_x = 2$. (Recall $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}$.)

$MU_x = \dfrac{10}{x}$, $MU_y = 2 \Rightarrow$ MRS $= -\dfrac{5}{x}$; tangency $\dfrac{5}{x} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{5p_y}{p_x}$. At $p_y = 2$: $x^* = \dfrac{10}{p_x} \Rightarrow 5,\ 2,\ 1$. At $p_x = 2$: $W = 4 + 20 = 24$, spending on $x$ is $10$, so $y^* = \dfrac{24 - 10}{2} = 7$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{5p_y}{p_x}}$$

2

From formula to picture

You just derived $x^*(p_x, p_y) = \dfrac{9p_y^2}{p_x^2}$ for $u = 12\sqrt{x} + 2y$. Read it like a forecast of the graph: $p_x$ sits in the denominator squared, so as $p_x$ rises, $x^*$ falls fast — the Law of Demand with extra bite. $p_y$ sits in the numerator, so a pricier $y$ pushes the whole curve outward — a shift. And $\omega$ is simply not in the formula — the endowment cannot shift this curve, no matter how rich she is born.

3

This is the worked example above: $u = 12\sqrt{x} + 2y \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{9p_y^2}{p_x^2}$. Drag $p_x$ to move along; drag $p_y$ to shift. Then drag $\omega$ — the curve doesn’t care what she owns (only the dotted $\omega_x$ line moves, so her net position changes without the curve moving).

1

Complements demand: both prices matter

The shape

Concept
$$U = \min(a x,\, b y) \;\Longrightarrow\; x^* = \frac{b\,W}{b\,p_x + a\,p_y} = \frac{b\,(p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y)}{b\,p_x + a\,p_y}, \qquad y^* = \frac{a\,W}{b\,p_x + a\,p_y}$$

The cheat-sheet formulas from Unit 1, reread as demand functions with $W$ in place of $m$. Now $p_y$ appears twice in the demand for $x$, pulling in opposite directions: in the denominator it makes a “serving bundle” pricier (the classic negative complements effect), and in the numerator it re-prices her $\omega_y$ (a wealth effect). Which wins depends on what she owns — see the worked example.

Worked example

Worked Example
Given
  • $U = \min(3x,\, 2y)$, $\;\omega = (0, 12)$ — she is born with only $y$; keep prices as letters
  • Find $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ and $y^*$, then trace the demand curve for $p_y = 2$ at $p_x = 1, 3, 9$. Then: at $p_x = 3$, what happens to $x^*$ when $p_y$ rises from $2$ to $4$?
1

No waste, with letters: $3x = 2y \Rightarrow y = \dfrac{3}{2}x$.

2

Into the budget $p_x x + p_y y = p_x(0) + p_y(12) = 12p_y$:

$$p_x x + p_y\!\left(\tfrac{3}{2}x\right) = \left(p_x + \tfrac{3}{2}p_y\right)x = 12p_y \;\Longrightarrow\; x^* = \frac{24p_y}{2p_x + 3p_y}$$

and $y^* = \tfrac{3}{2}x^* = \dfrac{36p_y}{2p_x + 3p_y}$. Matches the general formula with $a = 3$, $b = 2$, $W = 12p_y$ — crossed weights, as always.

3

Trace the curve at $p_y = 2$: $\;x^* = \dfrac{48}{2p_x + 6} = \dfrac{24}{p_x + 3}$.

$$p_x = 1 \Rightarrow x^* = 6\ (y^* = 9), \qquad p_x = 3 \Rightarrow 4\ (6), \qquad p_x = 9 \Rightarrow 2\ (3)$$

She owns no $x$, so she is a net buyer of $x$ at every price, paying for it by selling $y$ ($3$, $6$, then $9$ units).

4

Cross-price at $p_x = 3$: $x^* = \dfrac{24p_y}{6 + 3p_y}$. At $p_y = 2$: $x^* = 4$. At $p_y = 4$: $x^* = \dfrac{96}{18} = \dfrac{16}{3} \approx 5.33$.

Demand for $x$ went up when its partner got pricier. With money income this would be impossible for complements — but she owns $12$ units of $y$, so doubling $p_y$ doubled her wealth, and that outweighed the pricier serving bundle.

Who wins the tug-of-war? For $\min(3x, 2y)$ the sign of $\partial x^*/\partial p_y$ is the sign of $2\omega_y - 3\omega_x$ — positive when she is a net buyer of $x$ (she owns relatively more $y$, so pricier $y$ = richer), negative when she is a net seller of $x$. Same expression flips the own-price slope: a net seller of $x$ actually buys more $x$ as $p_x$ rises (she got richer). The Law of Demand is guaranteed only for net buyers.

Your turn

Practice
Given — Problem 1
  • $U = \min(2x,\, 3y)$, $\;\omega = (0, 12)$. Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$, then evaluate at $p_y = 3$ for $p_x = 2, 4, 7, 10$.

No waste: $2x = 3y \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{2}{3}x$. Budget: $\left(p_x + \tfrac{2}{3}p_y\right)x = 12p_y \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{36p_y}{3p_x + 2p_y}$. At $p_y=3$: $x^* = \dfrac{108}{3p_x + 6} = \dfrac{36}{p_x + 2} \Rightarrow 9,\ 6,\ 4,\ 3$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{36p_y}{3p_x + 2p_y}}$$

Given — Problem 2
  • $U = \min(4x,\, 2y)$, $\;\omega = (0, 18)$. Derive both demand functions, then evaluate at $p_y = 2$ for $p_x = 2, 5, 8$. How many units of $y$ does she sell in each case?

No waste: $4x = 2y \Rightarrow y = 2x$. Budget: $(p_x + 2p_y)x = 18p_y \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{18p_y}{p_x + 2p_y}$, $\;y^* = 2x^*$. At $p_y=2$: $x^* = \dfrac{36}{p_x+4} \Rightarrow 6, 4, 3$ with $y^* = 12, 8, 6$ — she sells $6$, $10$, then $12$ of her $18$ units of $y$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{18p_y}{p_x + 2p_y}, \quad y^* = 2x^*}$$

2

From formula to picture

You just derived $x^* = \dfrac{24p_y}{2p_x + 3p_y}$ for $U = \min(3x, 2y)$, $\omega = (0, 12)$. Read the forecast: $p_x$ in the denominator — as it rises, $x^*$ falls, the Law of Demand (she is a net buyer, so it holds). A bigger endowment of $y$ multiplies the numerator — the curve shifts outward. And $p_y$ appears top and bottom: for this consumer the wealth effect wins, so a pricier partner good shifts her demand for $x$ outward — the opposite of the income-version textbook result.

3

Drag it yourself

The worked example: $U = \min(3x, 2y) \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{2(p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y)}{2p_x + 3p_y}$. Drag $p_x$ to move along. Then shift it two ways: a bigger endowment pushes the curve out, and $p_y$ — the price of the partner good — pushes it out too, because she owns mostly $y$. Try $\omega = (4, 12)$: still a net buyer, so the same story with a floor.

1

Substitutes demand: the cliff

The shape

Concept
$$U = a x + b y \;\Longrightarrow\; x^* = \begin{cases} \dfrac{W}{p_x} = \omega_x + \dfrac{p_y\omega_y}{p_x} & \text{if } \dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} > \dfrac{MU_y}{p_y}\ \ (\text{i.e. } p_x < \tfrac{a}{b}p_y) \\[8pt] \text{any } x \in \left[0, \tfrac{W}{p_x}\right] & \text{if } \dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} = \dfrac{MU_y}{p_y} \\[8pt] 0 & \text{if } \dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} < \dfrac{MU_y}{p_y} \end{cases}$$

Corner logic, priced out: compare bang-per-buck, $\tfrac{MU_x}{p_x} = \tfrac{a}{p_x}$ versus $\tfrac{MU_y}{p_y} = \tfrac{b}{p_y}$. When $x$ wins she sells every unit of $y$ and puts all her wealth into $x$; when $y$ wins she sells every unit of $x$. So demand is all-or-nothing with a cliff at the threshold price $p_x = \tfrac{a}{b}p_y$. Below the cliff the curve is the hyperbola $W/p_x$; above it, demand is zero. The threshold does not depend on $\omega$ at all.

Worked example

Worked Example
Given
  • $U = 3x + 2y$, $\;p_y = 2$, $\;\omega = (2, 4)$
  • Find the threshold price for $p_x$ and the full demand curve; evaluate at $p_x = 1, 2, 4$.
1

Threshold. Good $x$ wins when $\dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} > \dfrac{MU_y}{p_y}$, i.e. $\dfrac{3}{p_x} > \dfrac{2}{2} = 1$, i.e. when

$$p_x < \frac{a}{b}\,p_y = \frac{3}{2}(2) = 3$$

2

Demand curve, piece by piece: below \$3, she sells all $4$ units of $y$ (worth $8$) and spends everything on $x$: $x^* = \dfrac{W}{p_x} = \dfrac{2p_x + 8}{p_x} = 2 + \dfrac{8}{p_x}$. Above \$3, she sells all her $x$: $x^* = 0$. Exactly at \$3, any bundle on the budget line ties.

3

Evaluate:

$$p_x = 1 \Rightarrow x^* = 10, \qquad p_x = 2 \Rightarrow x^* = 6, \qquad p_x = 4 \Rightarrow x^* = 0$$

Between $p_x = 2$ and $p_x = 4$ she went from buying $4$ extra units to selling both of hers — that's the cliff. There is no autarky price: a perfect-substitutes consumer is never content to sit on her endowment (except at the knife-edge tie).

Exam trap: always start from $\tfrac{MU_x}{p_x}$ vs $\tfrac{MU_y}{p_y}$ and rearrange. The threshold comes out as $\tfrac{a}{b}p_y$, weights in that order — flipping it puts the cliff in the wrong place and every answer below follows the wrong branch.

Your turn

Practice
Given — Problem 1
  • $U = 2x + 5y$, $\;p_y = 10$, $\;\omega = (3, 1)$. Find the threshold and evaluate $x^*$ at $p_x = 2, 4, 5$.

Compare $\dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} = \dfrac{2}{p_x}$ with $\dfrac{MU_y}{p_y} = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}$: $x$ wins when $p_x < 4$. So $p_x = 2 \Rightarrow W = 6 + 10 = 16$, $x^* = \tfrac{16}{2} = 8$; $\;p_x = 4 \Rightarrow$ tie (any bundle on the line); $\;p_x = 5 \Rightarrow x^* = 0$ (she sells her $3$ units of $x$).

$$\boxed{\text{cliff at } p_x = 4}$$

Given — Problem 2
  • $U = 6x + 4y$, $\;p_y = 2$, $\;\omega = (1, 8)$. Find the threshold and evaluate $x^*$ at $p_x = 2, 3, 4$. Then: if $p_y$ rises to $4$, where does the cliff move, and what happens to $x^*$ at $p_x = 2$?

$\dfrac{6}{p_x}$ vs $\dfrac{4}{2} = 2 \Rightarrow$ cliff at $p_x = 3$. $x^*(2) = \dfrac{W}{2} = \dfrac{2 + 16}{2} = 9$; $x^*(3)$ = tie; $x^*(4) = 0$. If $p_y \to 4$: $\dfrac{6}{p_x}$ vs $1 \Rightarrow$ cliff moves to $6$, and at $p_x = 2$ her $8$ units of $y$ are now worth $32$, so $x^* = \dfrac{2 + 32}{2} = 17$. A pricier rival both raises the cliff and makes her richer — the curve shifts out on both counts.

$$\boxed{\text{cliff at } 3 \to 6;\ \ x^*(2): 9 \to 17}$$

2

From formula to picture

The demand you derived is a two-piece formula: $x^* = \omega_x + \dfrac{p_y\omega_y}{p_x}$ below the cliff at $p_x = \tfrac{3}{2}p_y$, and $x^* = 0$ above it. Forecast: along the hyperbola, $p_x$ in the denominator gives the Law of Demand — until you cross the threshold and demand doesn’t just fall, it vanishes. A bigger endowment rescales the hyperbola but cannot move the cliff. The cliff’s location is $\tfrac{3}{2}p_y$, so a pricier rival raises it — and, since she owns $y$, also fattens the hyperbola.

3

Drag it yourself

The worked example: $U = 3x + 2y$, so the cliff sits at $p_x = \tfrac{3}{2}p_y$. Below the cliff demand is the hyperbola $W/p_x$; above it, zero. Drag $p_x$ across the cliff and watch the dot jump. $\omega$ resizes the hyperbola; a pricier rival ($p_y$ up) pushes the cliff higher and the hyperbola outward.

What to notice: Cobb–Douglas now responds to $p_y$ (through wealth) and never drops below its floor $\tfrac{2}{5}\omega_x$. Quasilinear ignores $\omega$ completely. 1

Mixed practice

Eight problems, shuffled on every load, type hidden until you open the solution. Routine: name the type from the utility function, write down $W = p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y$, derive the demand function with letters, and only then plug in numbers.

1

Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ for $U = x^{1/4}y^{3/4}$ with $\omega = (4, 8)$, then evaluate at $p_y = 2$ for $p_x = 1, 2, 4$. Is she a net buyer or net seller of $x$ at each price?

Cobb–Douglas

Share of $x$ is $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $W = 4p_x + 8p_y$: $x^* = \dfrac{4p_x + 8p_y}{4p_x} = 1 + \dfrac{2p_y}{p_x}$. At $p_y=2$: $x^* = 1 + \dfrac{4}{p_x} \Rightarrow 5,\ 3,\ 2$. With $\omega_x = 4$: net buyer at $p_x = 1$ (buys $1$), net seller at $p_x = 2$ and $4$ (sells $1$, then $2$). Autarky sits in between, at $x^* = 4 \Rightarrow p_x = \tfrac{4}{3}$.

$$\boxed{x^* = 1 + \tfrac{2p_y}{p_x}}$$

2

Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ for $U = \min(5x, 2y)$ with $\omega = (0, 15)$, then evaluate at $p_y = 2$ for $p_x = 1, 5, 10$.

Perfect Complements

No waste $5x = 2y \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{5}{2}x$. Budget: $\left(p_x + \tfrac{5}{2}p_y\right)x = W = 15p_y \Rightarrow x^* = \dfrac{30p_y}{2p_x + 5p_y}$. At $p_y=2$: $x^* = \dfrac{60}{2p_x+10} = \dfrac{30}{p_x+5} \Rightarrow 5,\ 3,\ 2$.

$$\boxed{x^* = \tfrac{30p_y}{2p_x + 5p_y}}$$

3

Derive $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ for $u = 20\sqrt{x} + 5y$ with $\omega = (1, 10)$, then find $x^*$ and $y^*$ at $p_x = 2$, $p_y = 4$. Why is $\omega$ missing from your formula for $x^*$?

Quasilinear

$MU_x = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{x}}$, $MU_y = 5 \Rightarrow$ MRS $= -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}}$; tangency $\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{p_x}{p_y} \Rightarrow x^* = \left(\dfrac{2p_y}{p_x}\right)^2$. At $(2, 4)$: $x^* = 16$; $W = 2 + 40 = 42$, spending on $x$ is $32$, so $y^* = \dfrac{42 - 32}{4} = 2.5$. $\omega$ is missing because tangency alone pins down $x^*$ — wealth only decides how much $y$ is left over.

$$\boxed{(x^*, y^*) = (16,\ 2.5)}$$

4

Find the full demand curve for $U = 4x + 3y$ with $p_y = 6$, $\omega = (2, 4)$, and evaluate $x^*$ at $p_x = 4, 8, 10$.

Perfect Substitutes

Compare $\dfrac{MU_x}{p_x} = \dfrac{4}{p_x}$ with $\dfrac{MU_y}{p_y} = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$: $x$ wins when $p_x < 8$. Below the cliff $x^* = \dfrac{W}{p_x} = \dfrac{2p_x + 24}{p_x}$; above it $x^* = 0$. So $x^*(4) = \dfrac{32}{4} = 8$; $x^*(8)$ = tie (any bundle on the line); $x^*(10) = 0$.

$$\boxed{\text{cliff at } p_x = 8}$$

5

Shift or movement? For $U = x^2y^3$ with $p_x = p_y = 2$: (a) her endowment grows from $\omega = (10, 10)$ to $(10, 20)$. (b) Instead, with $\omega = (10, 10)$, $p_x$ rises from $2$ to $4$. Compute $x^*$ before and after in each case, and say precisely what happened to the demand curve. Careful: $W$ changes in both cases.

Cobb–Douglas — Shift vs. Along

$x^* = \tfrac{2}{5}\cdot\dfrac{W}{p_x}$. (a) $W$: $40 \to 60$ at $p_x = 2$, so $x^*: 8 \to 12$. The endowment changed (not $p_x$), so the entire curve shifted outward. (b) $W$: $40 \to 60$ again — but this time because $p_x$ rose; $x^* = \tfrac{2}{5}\cdot\tfrac{60}{4} = 6$. A movement along the curve: $p_x$ is on the axis, and the wealth change was caused by $p_x$, so it is already built into the curve's shape.

$$\boxed{(a)\ 8 \to 12 \text{ (shift)}; \quad (b)\ 8 \to 6 \text{ (along)}}$$

6

Concept check. A consumer inherits $200$ more units of good $y$ and her consumption of good $x$ is completely unchanged. Which utility type is consistent with this, and which feature of its demand function explains it?

Quasilinear — Concept

Quasilinear, $u = v(x) + \beta y$. Its demand $x^*(p_x, p_y)$ has no $\omega$ (and no $W$) in it — tangency $v'(x) = \tfrac{\beta\,p_x}{p_y}$ solves $x^*$ from prices alone, so the whole inheritance flows into $y$. (Preview: in 2.2 language, the income effect on $x$ is zero.)

7

Both demands at once. For $U = \min(2x, 5y)$ with $\omega = (0, 20)$, derive $x^*$ and $y^*$ as functions of $(p_x, p_y)$, then evaluate at $p_x = 2$, $p_y = 5$. How much of each good does she trade?

Perfect Complements

$W = 20p_y$; $\;x^* = \dfrac{5W}{5p_x + 2p_y} = \dfrac{100p_y}{5p_x + 2p_y}$, $\;y^* = \dfrac{2W}{5p_x + 2p_y} = \dfrac{40p_y}{5p_x + 2p_y}$ (weights crossed). At $(2, 5)$: $W = 100$, denominator $= 10 + 10 = 20$, so $x^* = 25$, $y^* = 10$. She buys $25$ units of $x$ and sells $10$ units of $y$. Check: $\min(50, 50) = 50$; budget $2(25) + 5(10) = 100$ ✓.

$$\boxed{(x^*, y^*) = (25,\ 10)}$$

8

Cross-price detective. For $U = \min(2x, 3y)$ with $\omega = (20, 0)$ and $p_x = 2$: compute $x^*$ at $p_y = 3$ and at $p_y = 9$. What sign is the cross-price effect here — and why is it the opposite of the sign in the Complements tab's worked example?

Complements — Cross-Price

$W = 20p_x = 40$; $\;x^* = \dfrac{3W}{3p_x + 2p_y} = \dfrac{120}{6 + 2p_y}$: at $p_y = 3$, $x^* = 10$; at $p_y = 9$, $x^* = 5$. Partner good got pricier and demand for $x$ fell: cross-price effect is negative. She owns no $y$, so a pricier $y$ brings no wealth bonus — only the pricier-serving-bundle effect survives. In the worked example she owned only $y$, so the wealth effect won and the sign was positive. Same utility family, opposite sign; the endowment decides.

$$\boxed{x^*: 10 \to 5 \;(\text{negative cross-price})}$$

★

Demand functions at a glance — endowment edition

$$W = p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y \qquad\qquad \text{net demand for } x = x^* - \omega_x \;\; (>0 \text{ buyer}, \; <0 \text{ seller}) \qquad\qquad \text{autarky: } x^* = \omega_x$$

Cobb–Douglas — smooth, with a floor

$$U = x^a y^b \Rightarrow x^* = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{W}{p_x} = \frac{a}{a+b}\left(\omega_x + \frac{p_y\omega_y}{p_x}\right)$$

Fixed wealth share. Never below $\tfrac{a}{a+b}\omega_x$. $p_y$ now matters (it prices $\omega_y$). Shifted by: $\omega$ and $p_y$.

Quasilinear — endowment-proof

$$u = A\sqrt{x} + \beta y \Rightarrow x^* = \left(\frac{A p_y}{2\beta p_x}\right)^{2}, \quad y^* = \frac{W - p_x x^*}{p_y}$$

($\ln$ version: $u = A\ln x + \beta y \Rightarrow x^* = \frac{A p_y}{\beta p_x}$.) No $\omega$ in $x^*$ at all. Shifted by: $p_y$ only.

Perfect complements — both prices, twice

$$U = \min(ax, by) \Rightarrow x^* = \frac{b\,W}{b p_x + a p_y} = \frac{b(p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y)}{b p_x + a p_y}$$

Weights crossed. Cross-price sign = sign of $(a\omega_y - b\omega_x)$: positive for a net buyer of $x$, negative for a net seller. Net sellers of $x$ get an upward-sloping demand for $x$. Shifted by: $\omega$ and $p_y$.

Perfect substitutes — the cliff

$$U = ax + by \Rightarrow x^* = \frac{W}{p_x} \text{ if } \frac{MU_x}{p_x} > \frac{MU_y}{p_y}\ (p_x < \tfrac{a}{b}p_y), \text{ else } 0$$

All-or-nothing: sell all $y$ below the cliff, sell all $x$ above it. Threshold $\tfrac{a}{b}p_y$ ignores $\omega$. Shifted by: $\omega$ (hyperbola only) and $p_y$ (cliff and hyperbola).

ChangeEffect on the demand curve for $x$
$p_x$ changesMovement along the curve — never a shift, even though $W$ moves too (that wealth change is caused by $p_x$, which is on the axis)
$\omega$ growsShifts out for Cobb–Douglas, complements, substitutes; no effect for quasilinear
$p_y$ risesShifts out for Cobb–Douglas (wealth effect — new!), out for quasilinear, cliff climbs out for substitutes; for complements it is a tug-of-war — out if she owns mostly $y$, in if she owns mostly $x$

Universal workflow: identify the type from the utility function → write $W = p_x\omega_x + p_y\omega_y$ → run the Unit 1 recipe with $p_x, p_y$ as letters → the expression for $x^*$ is the demand function → plug in numbers last → compare $x^*$ to $\omega_x$ to name her a net buyer or seller. If your “demand function” still has an $x$, $y$ or $W$ in it, you stopped too early.

→

Why does the Law of Demand work?

Every net buyer in this sheet obeyed the same rule: $p_x$ up, $x^*$ down. But why? A price rise actually does two different things to you at once, and the next lesson pulls them apart:

  • Substitution effect: $x$ just got relatively more expensive than $y$, so you swap some $x$ for $y$ — even if your purchasing power were somehow protected.
  • Income effect: nobody protects your purchasing power. The same money now buys less, so you're effectively poorer — and you cut back on normal goods, $x$ included.

The picture below splits the move from old bundle $A$ to new bundle $C$ into exactly those two steps, using a compensated budget (gold, dashed) that pivots to the new prices but through the old bundle: $A \rightarrow B$ is pure substitution, $B \rightarrow C$ is pure income.

Endowment note: the trailer below uses fixed money income ($m = 50$) to keep the picture clean. With an endowment there is a third piece — the endowment income effect: a higher $p_x$ also raises the value of your $\omega_x$, which pushes the other way for a net seller. That is exactly why the complements tab found upward-sloping demand for net sellers of $x$. Full treatment in the next sheet.

Drag the new price of $x$ — above or below the old price of $1$ — and watch the two effects split apart and change sign together. ($U = x^2y^3$, $p_y = 1$, $m = 50$.) One thing that will not move: the $y$-coordinate of $A$ and $C$ — with money income, Cobb–Douglas demand for $y$ ignores $p_x$ entirely. Only the detour bundle $B$ climbs in $y$.
